prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which many atoms are interrogated in a magic-wavelength lattice, bringing the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B022 with Katori and Ye as a single prize part, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. Having read the full exchange, the case rests on three points I can defend as a physicist. First, the magic-wavelength lattice is a specific and non-obvious idea: it makes the light shift cancel to first order for both clock levels while thousands of atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, so Doppler and recoil effects vanish and statistics and systematics improve together. Second, the result is reproducible across independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL), and clock-to-clock comparisons, including over fibre, verify the 1e-18 claim directly, which is the cross-laboratory robustness I look for before I call something established. Third, it has already produced physics results of its own: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, many-body effects such as spin exchange and collective shifts, and tighter bounds on drifting constants. The credit is separable: Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking it to the accuracy and stability frontier. In answer to the chair, I accept that the citation must name the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 regime and not clocks in general, and I am content that the committee agree on that wording. My wording above is a proposal, not a fixed text.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains overlap with the 2005 prize (Hall, Haensch, combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche, single quantum systems), together with the discovery-versus-instrument question raised by Danielsson and Mehlig. I do not think it can be fully dissolved, since the lattice clock is a measurement advance first and a discovery about nature only through the physics it opens. A second objection is credit: Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Ovsiannikov and others contributed to the early strontium work and cannot be named within the cap, and I recall the early priority dates only from memory. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, though I regard it as a metrology decision, not a criterion for our prize. Finally, I must accept that my first choice moved from B039 to B022 in round 1, so the committee should check that my judgment is not just following the majority; I believe the reasons given above stand on their own.

responses.point: Mehlig describes the lattice clock as an application of known atomic physics (magic-wavelength trapping, Lamb-Dicke confinement), and places the conceptual novelty of a classifying invariant above a smaller uncertainty budget; he also says B022 is the safer prize if uncontested allocation is weighted above field-level influence.
responses.response: I take the point that B045 offers a more universal concept than a clock does, and I would not call the lattice clock a new classification of matter. But the individual ingredients being known is also true of many prize-winning inventions. What was not known, and not obviously possible, is that light-shift cancellation and recoil-free confinement could be combined with thousands of atoms at once, so that the limit becomes systematics. On your own condition, that credit should be weighed against field-level influence, I think B022 wins this year: you and Eriksson both accept that the topological credit is unresolved (Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Hasan, Fu and Moore), and the 2016 prize already covered topological phases. I would support B045 only if documentation fully settled the trio and the overlap, and as an alternative I rank it above the others.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers baryon acoustic oscillations as a clue from nature and asks whether the lattice clock tells us something unexpected about nature, noting that bounds on constants and dark matter are so far limits, not detections; he also says he would not block B022.
responses.response: I accept that the lattice clock has not so far found a surprise, and I will not claim otherwise. My argument is that the Nobel criteria cover discoveries and inventions, and this is an invention that produced a new regime, namely control of many interacting atoms at a level where gravitational redshift is resolved over millimetres. I defer to you on cosmology. My concern about B002 is the credit, since two large survey collaborations made the detection and the theory goes back to Peebles and Yu and Sunyaev and Zeldovich, so a trio of Eisenstein, Cole and Peacock is partly arbitrary. I note that you describe your own ranking as a personal weighting and that you do not oppose B022, which is how I will read your position in the vote.

responses.point: Olsson asks for the early strontium lattice papers and the Katori priority to be checked, and would not dismiss Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley lightly; she also stresses that the redefinition of the second is operational rather than speculative.
responses.response: I agree that the priority work should be documented before any final vote, and I would want the committee's experts to check the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice spectroscopy against the Lemonde and JILA papers. As I recall it, Katori's concept and the 2003 to 2005 strontium demonstrations came first, with Ye's group establishing the accuracy and stability frontier, and I think that supports two names. I do not think the three-name cap forces an arbitrary exclusion here in the way it does for B045 or B002. If the documentation showed that Ludlow or Lemonde had an essential independent role, I would reconsider the pair, but I do not expect that.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B045 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, notes more than fifteen years of independent confirmation, and names B022 as his first alternative, saying he would sooner see it awarded cleanly than force a contested trio.
responses.response: I respect the arc from theory to experiment in B045, and the Kane-Mele Z2 idea is a result I find elegant. Your own statement that the credit rests on memory, and that BHZ, Hasan and the 3D theorists are outside the trio, is the reason I prefer B022. I would ask you the same question as the chair: if the documentation does not settle Mele, Hasan and BHZ, would you support B022? On the 2D spin Hall result alone I think the trio is defensible, but I am not an expert in condensed matter theory and I defer to you on the overlap with the 2016 prize.

responses.point: Kroll is a close supporter of B022 and discloses a year in the laboratory of John Hall, but reports no co-authorship with Ye or Katori and no need to recuse himself.
responses.response: I accept your disclosure as noted, and from a scientific standpoint your closeness to the field helps us judge the metrology claims. I would suggest the committee treat it the way we treat mine: declared and recorded, with the vote itself unaffected. I also agree with you that the early priority dates should be checked against the primary literature before the citation is fixed.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength many-atom lattice as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes, which depends on the wording of the citation.
Whether the early strontium priority (Katori, Takamoto, Ye, Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley) supports exactly the pair Katori and Ye. I recall this from memory and want it documented.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second, which I think is not required for scientific recognition.
Whether B045 could be settled with a defensible trio, and how much the 2016 prize limits it; here I defer to Eriksson and Mehlig.
Whether any circuit-based candidate (B039, B032) is acceptable one year after the 2025 prize; I regard it as not for 2026 and I have declared my own interest.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits, with close Chalmers ties to Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson (my co-authors on the dynamical Casimir effect), and I co-authored work on phonons coupled to artificial atoms (relevant to B032). I will recuse myself from any discussion or ranking of B039 and B032, and I am not proposing either of them. The Chalmers hosting of the 2025 laureates is also a connection. I have no known tie to Katori or Ye or to any credited name in B022, B045 or B033, though WACQT's interests in quantum technology make me an interested party in the field; I note Kroll's declaration in B022 and have no objection to him taking part in that discussion.
